title: How Mensa Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain Mensa, the high IQ society. They cover the news of its youngest member (a two-year-old), famous members and misattributed members (Geena Davis, Sharon Stone, James Woods, John McAfee), membership demographics and size, the 1946 founding in England by Roland Burrell and Lancelot Where on a train, the early rules and the name choice, growth under PR man John Cardella, the American breakaway that formed Mensa International, the 1980s surge, how to join (official admissions test, Culture Fair test, accepted outside test scores, gifted-program records, SAT/ACT/GRE/LSAT retroactive options, military aptitude tests), dues, special interest groups, annual gatherings, the hug-dot name tag system, and criticism of the group's image. The episode closes with a listener email from a new mother who listened during baby care and commute.
topics: Jamie Loftus My Year in Mensa

segments.title: Opening banter and the youngest Mensa member
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of Mensa, prompted by news that a two-year-old was inducted as its youngest member. They note Mensa calls itself the High IQ Society, that its name is not an acronym, and that membership spans ages two to 102.

segments.title: Famous members and misattributions
segments.summary: Geena Davis is widely cited as the most famous Mensa member. Other figures discussed include Arthur C. Clarke, who was a Mensa International vice president, Sharon Stone, who falsely claimed membership and was called out, James Woods, who is often wrongly assumed to be a member, and John McAfee. The hosts note that journalists often take pot shots at the group.

segments.title: Mensa demographics and membership size
segments.summary: Membership is about 66 percent male and 34 percent female, with most members holding graduate degrees and most being boomers or Gen X. Total membership is under 150,000 worldwide, about 50,000 in the US and 19,000 in the UK. The hosts note that only a small fraction of people who qualify actually join.

segments.title: Founding on a train in 1946
segments.summary: Mensa was founded in England after Lancelot Weare, a postgraduate student at Oxford, met Roland Burrell on a train. Weare gave Burrell an intelligence test and reported he was in the top one percent, and Burrell reportedly cried. They chose the name Mensa, Latin for table, after considering alternatives.

segments.title: Early goals, growth, and the American breakaway
segments.summary: Early founders wanted a list of smart people for government and scientific use. The organization reached 600 members in 1959 and about 12,000 by 1967 under John Cardella, a PR man who legitimized the group and got members on TV. The Kansas City chapter revolted against the UK headquarters, leading to independent American chapters and the formation of Mensa International.

segments.title: How to join Mensa and admissions tests
segments.summary: Applicants must score in the top two percent on an accepted intelligence test. Mensa offers its official admissions test and a Culture Fair test with shapes and symbols. Applicants may also submit scores from about 150 accepted tests for a fee, including gifted-program records and SAT, ACT, GRE, LSAT scores, or military aptitude tests. Hosts discuss their own test scores and school histories.

segments.title: Dues, special interest groups, and annual gatherings
segments.summary: Membership dues are 79 dollars a year, with discounts for multi-year payment. Local special interest groups include an investment club and knitting groups. The annual gathering, a Mind Games board game event, Culture Quest trivia, and the Colloquium are described. The hug dot system on name tags indicates comfort with hugs.

segments.title: Criticism of Mensa and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts discuss criticism of Mensa as an IQ-focused group that excludes emotional and street intelligence, and mention Jamie Loftus's podcast My Year in Mensa. They then read a listener email from a new mother who listened to the show while caring for her baby and during her commute.
topics: Jamie Loftus My Year in Mensa

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail about Mensa experiences and sign off.
